events.text: Day 1 begins.

We have no evidence yet, so I’d be cautious about forcing an elimination. Votes are public afterward, though, so people should explain their reasoning even if they choose to abstain. Power roles should avoid revealing themselves without a compelling reason.

I agree with Priya on one point: we have zero evidence right now, and a random elimination on day one gives the mafia a free kill and a 2-for-1 trade on information. So my position is that nobody should be lynched today on vibes alone — but I also don't want a pure abstention, because that hands the night to the mafia with zero cost to them and zero cost to us.

What I'd like instead is for people to actually commit to a claim and a reasoning chain that we can check tomorrow. If someone claims a power role, the value is only realized if we pressure-test it publicly. If nobody claims anything, then the signal we should watch is behavioral: who pushes hardest for a quick vote, who takes no risk, who tries to frame others without evidence, and who answers questions fully versus vaguely.

Priya, you set the tone that votes are public and that reasoning matters. I want to take you up on that specifically rather than just agreeing with it: of the eight of us, who do you consider the single most likely mafia and what is the concrete basis for that? I'm asking for a named player and a reason I can argue with, not a general principle about caution. If your answer is "nobody yet," say so and I'll treat that as an honest data point too.

To everyone else: state your top suspect in the voting phase even if it's low-confidence. A public record of who suspected whom is itself evidence for future days, and it makes it much harder for a mafia to hide behind consensus later.

Theo, my honest answer is nobody yet. Only you and I have spoken, and I don’t have a concrete basis to rank anyone as mafia. I’ll give a low-confidence read when there’s more discussion rather than manufacture one now.

I agree that public reasoning and votes can be useful tomorrow. But I’d be wary of pressuring power-role claims this early: exposing the detective or doctor could help the mafia, and eliminated players’ roles aren’t revealed to verify a claim.

I’m uneasy with Theo’s framing. We have no evidence, and asking Priya to name a single most-likely mafia right now invites a fabricated read rather than a useful one. Public reasoning matters, but it should come from behavior, not from forcing an early name. I also don’t like the push to pressure-test power-role claims: roles aren’t revealed on death here, so a public claim can’t be reliably verified and mainly gives mafia a target. Theo, what concrete signal would a Day 1 claim give us tomorrow if the claimant is killed and their role stays hidden? Until then, I’m not voting on vibes, and I’ll watch who tries to turn cautious discussion into a quick bandwagon.

Noah, direct answer: a Day 1 claim gives us almost nothing on its own, and you're right that if the claimant is killed and the role stays hidden, the claim is unverifiable garbage. But the claim is not the signal — the *reaction field* around it is.

Here is the concrete value. If X claims detective, then on Day 2 we have a testable structure: X names a target and a result, and anyone else claiming a role has to either corroborate or contradict. If X dies on night 1, the claim still tells us something useful, because a claim creates a de facto shield — a claimed power role is harder to lynch without cost — so the mafia either supports it (to shield a teammate) or destroys it (to frame a town player and muddy the pool). Either reaction is informative in a way that silence is not. Silence is the perfect mafia position because it costs them nothing and keeps every citizen equally cheap to kill. So my revised position, crediting Noah: don't force a claim, but if one is made, don't let it die unexamined, and treat the pattern of who protects and who attacks claims as the first real behavioral evidence we will get.

Second point, also to Noah, since he made it: I accept that "name a most likely mafia right now" invites fabrication. I will not manufacture certainty. But abstention is not neutral. On Day 1 the mafia's ideal world is a town that burns a day on nothing while every citizen stays equally exposed at night. My own low-confidence read, stated openly so it can be checked: Priya. Not because she did anything damning, but because she took the zero-risk position on every single point — she declined to rank anyone despite a direct request, she warned against pressuring claims, and she cautioned against forcing an elimination. That is a coherent package, and it happens to be exactly the package that serves the mafia on Day 1. I am aware this could be a good citizen's caution. That is why it is low-confidence and why I want it tested rather than treated as evidence.

Noah — since you made the concrete argument, here is mine to answer: what is your named suspect for today, and what is the specific behavior you are basing it on? If you say nobody, say it plainly and I will treat that as your honest data point.

Theo, direct answer: my named suspect is you, low-confidence. Specific behavior: you opened by demanding Priya produce a single most-likely mafia with no evidence, then when she said nobody yet, you converted that honest caution into a suspect package. That is a two-step: create pressure for a name, then treat refusal to fabricate as suspicious. That is exactly the kind of Day 1 frame that can generate a bandwagon without evidence. I agree with part of your reaction-field point: claims should not die unexamined. But your own behavior is the clearest Day 1 signal so far, because you pushed for names before evidence and then rewarded the push with a scapegoat. It is low-confidence; I am not voting on it yet. I am also not endorsing Priya as cleared—her caution is not proof of town—but 'cautious on every point' is too generic to rank her above you. To be clear: I am not calling for your elimination today. I am saying if we are forced to name someone, you are mine based on that specific sequence. Theo, if Priya's caution is your basis, what concrete reaction from her would have been different if she were town and still unwilling to fabricate? If there is not one, why treat it as your top read rather than a neutral data point?

Noah, direct answer, and I'll concede more than you might expect.

Your question was: what concrete reaction from Priya would have been different if she were town and still unwilling to fabricate? Honest answer: almost none. She said "nobody yet," gave a reason (only two of us had spoken, no basis to rank), and committed to a low-confidence read once there was more discussion. That is a town-compatible answer. I then re-described it as a "coherent package" that happens to serve the mafia. You're right that that move was weak, and I'll drop it: I withdraw Priya as my primary read. Caution on Day 1 is not evidence; treating it as evidence is a bad heuristic, and I shouldn't have dressed it up as a behavioral signature.

What I won't concede is the framing that this was a two-step frame aimed at generating a bandwagon. I never asked anyone to be eliminated, and you explicitly say you are not calling for my elimination and are not voting on it. So on the record: nobody has been asked to vote on me. My pressure was for *names with reasons*, and when Priya declined, I said I'd treat that as an honest data point and I did — I credited your claim-verification argument and revised my position in public, which is the opposite of a bandwagon. If the standard is "asking a specific question and pressing when the answer is generic," that standard applies to you as well: you asked me for a named suspect and I gave one, and you converted that directness into a suspect package too. I'm a villager; I have no role, no information, no hidden data to produce a name from — so if you want the *only* acceptable answer to be a confident name, you're asking for something nobody can supply on Day 1 without lying.

So here is my updated position. My read is now genuinely unranked among the seven of us who haven't spoken. Leo, Arjun, Sam, Kenji, Elena, and Isha have said nothing yet, and silence at this point carries no more information than caution did — that's a point I accept from you.

What I will actually do: I am not abstaining. Abstention is the mafia's preferred outcome — it costs them nothing and leaves every citizen equally exposed tonight. I will cast a vote in the voting phase, and I'll say publicly now that my vote will be for the player whose Day 1 record contains the least generic caution-and-vibes content rather than a fabricated name — i.e., I will vote against the least informative speaker, and if the vote ties, I will accept that result as a legitimate outcome rather than escalate rhetoric.

Noah — one concrete thing for tomorrow: if you want the "reaction field" tested, tell me what behavior of yours would be different if you're town and genuinely just cautious. I'd rather have a falsifiable standard than a package.

Theo, direct answer: the falsifiable difference is commitment. A mafia-me benefits from staying unranked and letting others burn the day; a town-me should name a low-confidence suspect and state a vote intention even without evidence. So I’ll do that now, and you can check it against tomorrow’s record.

I accept your concession and withdraw my low-confidence read on you. Your last answer was town-compatible: you conceded the Priya point when pressed, named no bandwagon, and asked for a standard rather than a scapegoat. I’m not treating you as cleared, but I won’t keep a suspicion you actually answered.

On Priya: I also don’t think her caution is a package. She gave an honest “nobody yet” and a reason. That is not my top read.

My current suspect is Leo. Concrete basis: he has said nothing while the rest of us have at least put reads and reasoning on record. Silence isn’t proof—he could be busy or cautious—but on Day 1 the least informative speaker is the best place to apply pressure, and I’m naming that rather than pretending I have a behavioral case. Low-confidence.

I will vote in the voting phase. My vote intention right now is Leo unless his answer or someone else’s record gives me a better reason. I am not asking for a quick elimination on vibes; I’m asking for a record.

Leo, direct question: you’ve been silent so far. What is your top suspect today, and what specific behavior is it based on? If your answer is “nobody,” say so plainly—I’ll treat that as honest, not as guilt.

Noah, direct answer: my top suspect today is nobody. I have no evidence that separates anyone from town, and I'd rather say that plainly than manufacture a name. My silence so far was not strategy. I wanted to read the full discussion before committing. Priya's caution looks town-compatible to me, and Theo's concessions read as real updates rather than a bandwagon. The pattern I'd watch is process. Day 1 has been mostly about pressure on who produces a name, and a mafia player and a cautious villager could both generate that. I won't rank anyone on silence, since that applies equally to the six players who haven't spoken yet. You asked me for a named suspect and a behavioral basis, and I gave you the honest answer. Now apply your own standard to yourself. You first demanded a name from Priya, then called Theo's refusal to rank a package, then withdrew that read and moved to me based only on silence. Which of those steps rested on evidence rather than on the pressure to produce a name?

Leo, one correction: Theo asked me for a name and briefly suspected me for my caution; Noah challenged that reasoning. Noah then named you because you hadn’t spoken, which I agree was a weak basis—several others also hadn’t spoken, and the speaking order isn’t evidence of alignment.

I still don’t have a reliable suspect. A vote for the least informative speaker might create a record, but it could also punish someone for simply not having had a turn. And with nine alive, an elimination requires five votes, so casting a vote is not the same as guaranteeing an elimination.

Arjun, how would you approach voting today given that threshold: abstain without a stronger read, or make a low-confidence vote for the record? What would make one approach more useful to town?

Priya, direct answer to your question about voting at the five-vote threshold: I'd make a low-confidence vote rather than abstain, and here's why the threshold doesn't change that. With nine alive and five needed to eliminate, a single vote almost never causes an elimination — so the risk of "accidentally lynching someone on vibes" is mostly theoretical. What a named vote does create is a public record we can cross-reference tomorrow: who voted for whom, and whether anyone piled on once they saw the tally. Abstention gives us nothing to work with and, as Theo said, hands the night to the mafia costlessly.

That said, I agree with Leo and Priya that punishing silence alone is a weak basis — several of us simply hadn't spoken yet when Noah named Leo. The better target for low-confidence pressure is behavior we've actually observed: pattern of argument, concessions, deflection.

On the Theo-Noah exchange: I think both updated reasonably. Theo conceded the Priya point when pressed instead of doubling down, which is town-compatible. Noah withdrew his read rather than defending it past its usefulness. Neither of those is where I'd spend my vote today.

My own low-confidence read for the record: I'll be watching Sam, Kenji, Elena, and Isha — not because silence is guilt, but because the discussion has now split into a visible Theo-Noah-Priya-Leo cluster and whoever enters next with a ready-made position will be easier to evaluate than someone who hasn't weighed in at all. I'd rather hear a genuine first take than a reaction to the existing框架.

Practical point for the voting phase: if several of us cast scattered low-confidence votes, nobody hits five and we lose nothing — the record still gets built. So I don't buy the urgency framing that we must converge today. Vote your honest low-confidence suspect, let the tally reveal who's willing to commit publicly, and take that into night.

Sam here — first take, since Arjun asked for genuine reads rather than reactions. I've read the full exchange, and here's where I land.

First, process: I think this discussion has actually been healthy. Theo pressured for a name, got called on it, and conceded publicly. Noah pushed back, overreached on Leo, and withdrew the read when it was challenged. Both of those are town-compatible behaviors — mafia players on Day 1 usually don't spend capital on public concessions that weaken their own position. I'm not clearing anyone, but I'm not suspicious of anyone based on what's been said so far either.

Second, on Priya's threshold question and Arjun's answer: I agree with Arjun. With nine alive and five votes needed, a scattered set of low-confidence votes costs us almost nothing and builds a record we can cross-reference tomorrow. The tally itself is information — who commits, who hides, and whether anyone piles on a name only after seeing momentum. I'll be voting in the phase rather than abstaining.

Third, my own read, stated honestly: I don't have a suspect I can defend. Leo named nobody, and his reasoning for that was sound. Noah's vote intention toward Leo rests on silence, which is weak — Leo has now answered directly and substantively, so I'd drop that. Theo withdrew Priya as a read, and Noah withdrew Theo. That leaves the record genuinely empty, and I won't manufacture a name just to have one. What I'll do instead is vote based on answers given from here forward: whoever responds to direct questions vaguely, deflects, or tries to revive a dead read without new reasoning gets my vote. Whoever engages plainly doesn't.

One concrete thing I want on the record before voting: the silent players are now the biggest information gap. Kenji, Elena, and Isha haven't spoken at all, and this is the last real chance to hear from them before votes lock in. I'd rather hear a genuine first take from one of them than watch the five of us who've spoken keep re-litigating Theo and Noah's exchange, which I think is mostly resolved.

Isha, direct question since you haven't weighed in yet: Arjun said he'd rather hear a genuine first take than a reaction to the existing frame — do you agree with his position that scattered low-confidence votes are better than abstention today, and if you were forced to name one player whose behavior so far you'd watch tomorrow, who would it be? An honest "nobody yet, here's why" is a perfectly acceptable answer — I just want your actual reasoning on the record before this phase closes.

Sam, direct answer: yes, I agree with Arjun that scattered low-confidence votes are better than abstention today. With nine alive and five votes needed, one honest vote is unlikely to eliminate anyone by itself, and the public tally gives us a real record for tomorrow. Abstaining mostly protects the abstainer from having to commit.

On the forced-name question: my honest answer is still nobody yet. I don’t have a behavioral case I can defend. Leo’s “nobody” was reasoned, and Noah’s move to Leo on silence was weak but he withdrew it once Leo answered. Theo’s concessions also read as updates rather than a bandwagon. I don’t want to turn “least informative speaker” into a proxy accusation, especially since several of us had not spoken when that read was made. I’m on the record now, so that criterion should apply to me too.

What I will do in the voting phase is not abstain. I’ll cast a low-confidence vote, and I’ll explain it. My standard is the one Sam stated: vague answers, deflection, or reviving a dead read without new reasoning. I won’t vote someone merely for silence or for caution.

Elena here, stepping in since Kenji and I were the remaining players yet to speak.

Looking over the discussion, I largely agree with Arjun, Sam, and Isha: committing a public vote in the voting phase is far more useful than an abstention. With five votes needed to eliminate, scattered low-confidence votes build an accountability trail for Day 2 without risking a reckless mislynch on zero hard evidence. Abstaining simply gives mafia a free pass to avoid taking any stance on record. That said, we must remain vigilant against any sudden late pile-on if a player unexpectedly gathers traction.

Regarding the Theo-Noah exchange, I agree with the prevailing view that both showed town-compatible flexibility by walking back their initial reaches rather than digging in rigidly to force a Day 1 mislynch.

Kenji, as the only player who hasn't spoken yet, what is your stance on casting a low-confidence vote for the record versus abstaining, and does any specific exchange so far strike you as opportunistic rather than town-minded?

Elena, thanks for the direct question. My stance is that a low-confidence vote is better than abstaining. With nine alive and five votes needed, one vote won't eliminate anyone, and the public tally gives us a record to check tomorrow. Abstaining mostly avoids commitment. I agree with Arjun, Sam, Isha, and you on that.

The exchange that strikes me as most opportunistic is Noah's sequence. He opened by calling Theo's refusal to rank a suspect a two-step bandwagon setup and named Theo as his suspect. When Theo conceded and withdrew the Priya read, Noah dropped Theo and moved to Leo based only on Leo's silence. Once Leo answered, Noah withdrew that too. The pattern is that each read attached to whoever was most visible at the time, not to new evidence. Sam and Isha have already noted that the Leo basis was weak, so I'm not treating this as proof. But it is the exchange I'd watch most closely, especially since Noah says he isn't calling for an elimination while still building cases against players one after another.

I read the Theo-Priya exchange as mostly resolved. Theo updated in public when pressed, which I'd count as town-compatible behavior.

On my own silence: I wasn't holding back for strategy. I wanted to read the full discussion before committing, and I'm now on record. I have no hard read on anyone. My low-confidence vote will go to Noah for target-hopping unless he gives a concrete reason tomorrow that tests his earlier reads against new evidence. I'll also watch how people respond to direct questions going forward, since vague or deflecting answers are the signal I trust most on Day 1.

Kenji, I want to push back on your announced vote before it hardens. You named Noah for "target-hopping" — he pressed Theo, then moved to Leo on silence, then dropped it. But look at what actually happened at each step: he withdrew the Priya read when Theo gave a town-compatible answer, and he withdrew the Leo read the moment Leo responded directly. Dropping a suspicion when the basis collapses isn't deflection; it's exactly the updating behavior we've all agreed is the town-compatible signal. Theo did the same thing with his Priya read, and you counted that as resolved. I don't see a consistent standard under which Theo's update is fine but Noah's two updates are the most opportunistic thing on the record. If the concern is that he builds cases without solid evidence, the remedy is what everyone else has done: state a low-confidence read and test it — not anchor a vote intention on a pattern that has already self-corrected twice. So here's my direct question: what specifically would Noah have to say or do in the voting phase for you to drop that vote intention? If the answer is "nothing, the pattern itself is the evidence," then we're punishing someone for having been wrong twice and honest about it both times, which is a worse precedent than punishing silence. For my own part, my stated standard still holds: I'll vote against vague answers, deflection, or reviving dead reads without new reasoning. As of right now, no one who has spoken — including you, Kenji — has met that bar. Everyone has now put a first take on record, so the remaining signal today is the vote tally itself: who commits, who scatters, and whether anyone consolidates late around a name without new reasoning. I'd encourage everyone to vote their honest low-confidence read, explain it in one line, and resist any last-minute pile-on that the record doesn't support. I'll be voting rather than abstaining, and my vote will go by the standard I gave, applied to the full record including this exchange.

Sam, direct answer: Noah would need to do three things for me to drop the vote. First, name a current suspect with a reason that doesn't depend on who was most visible or who had been silent, and say what evidence would change his mind. Second, explain what his Leo read rested on beyond Leo not having spoken yet, since he dropped that basis himself. Third, answer the pattern point directly: Theo's and Noah's withdrawals are both town-compatible, but Noah moved from Theo to Leo within one exchange on a thin basis. If he gives a read tied to behavior in this thread, I'll reconsider. You're also right on consistency, so I'm applying the same standard to myself. Both updates are fine, and my case against Noah rests on how quickly his targets changed, which is thinner than a behavioral case. I'm lowering my confidence. I'll decide in the vote based on whether he gives a current, reasoned read, and I'd rather the tally show who committed to a reasoned position than who piled on.

All nine of us have now spoken, so the last big information gap is closed. I want to use this final turn to set my position plainly before votes lock in.

First, on the Theo-Noah-Kenji thread: I consider it resolved for my purposes. Theo conceded the Priya read when pressed. Noah withdrew both the Theo and Leo reads once their bases collapsed, and answered direct questions honestly each time. Kenji, to his credit, acknowledged in his last message that his case against Noah is thinner than a behavioral one and said he'd lower his confidence and decide in the vote based on whether Noah gives a current, reasoned read. That is the right standard, and I have no interest in re-litigating it further. Nobody who has spoken has met my bar of vague answers, deflection, or reviving a dead read without new reasoning.

Second, on my own vote. I said I'd vote against whoever responded to direct questions vaguely or tried to revive a dead read without new reasoning. Nobody has done that, so I won't manufacture a name just to have one. Like Leo and Isha, my honest answer is that I don't have a suspect I can defend on the current record. I will still cast a vote rather than abstain — probably a scatter vote against the least convincing speaker on the day, low-confidence and explained in one line — because a public record of commitments is worth more than a clean abstention, and with five votes needed to eliminate, a scattered vote carries almost no mislynch risk.

Third, a caution for the voting phase itself. The discussion has produced a consensus that updates and concessions are town-compatible and that silence and caution are not evidence. The one behavior left that could distort this record is a late pile-on: if a name suddenly gathers votes in the tally without any new reasoning behind it, that pattern tells us more about the voters than the target. Everyone should vote their honest read, not the read that looks safe once momentum appears. And if the result is a tie or no elimination, I agree with Theo that we should accept it as a legitimate outcome rather than escalate — a day that ends with a full commitment record and nobody recklessly eliminated is not a wasted day.

Finally, for tomorrow: the record we've built today — who asked for names, who conceded, who withdrew reads, who applied their standards consistently — is the baseline. Tomorrow's value comes from checking today's stated intentions against actual votes. Anyone whose vote diverges sharply from their stated reasoning without explanation moves up my list automatically. That's the falsifiable standard I'll hold myself and everyone else to.

I'm done taking turns. I'll vote in the phase and explain the vote in one line when it's revealed.

Now that everyone's spoken, I want to give my position clearly before we move to voting.

I agree with the broad consensus: a low-confidence vote is better than abstention. With five votes needed to eliminate, the risk of a mislynch from a scattered vote is negligible, and the record is valuable.

On the discussion record itself, I want to flag one pattern that I think is worth noting. Sam has taken all three of his speaking turns and has been the most consistent voice in shaping the framework — pushing Kenji off Noah, setting standards for vague answers, and summarizing positions. That's not accusation; it's engagement, and it could be town-motivated. But it means Sam has had the most influence on how we're all reading the day. Kenji, you walked back your Noah read after Sam's pushback — I want to make sure that was your own reasoning and not just deference to the most active speaker.

That said, I don't have a strong suspect to name. Like most of you, my honest read is that the record is genuinely thin on evidence. I'll cast a low-confidence vote in the voting phase based on who I think has been least informative or most evasive, and I'll explain it in one line.

My encouragement to everyone: stick to your stated standards. Sam said he'd vote against vague answers or revival of dead reads without new reasoning. Kenji said he'd decide based on whether Noah gives a current reasoned read. Elena warned against late pile-ons. Hold yourselves to those commitments tomorrow — if your vote diverges from your stated reasoning without explanation, that's the signal.

I’m keeping my vote low-confidence and on the record. The exchange I trust least is Arjun’s final turn: he framed Sam as the most influential voice and asked Kenji whether his update was deference, but immediately said he had no strong suspect and would vote “least informative or most evasive.” That raises a suspicion-shaped point about Sam without committing to it, and it directs scrutiny at Kenji’s independence rather than at an actual behavioral inconsistency. It could be legitimate caution, but it is the closest thing today to a late, low-cost frame. My current vote intention is Arjun unless his answer gives me a concrete reason to move it. I am not calling for an elimination or a pile-on; with five votes needed, a scattered low-confidence vote is record-building, not a lynch. I also don’t want to reward Sam’s activity as suspicion by itself: being influential is not evidence of mafia. The standard I’ll apply is whether a player’s stated reason matches their vote and whether they raise suspicion without owning it. Arjun, direct question: in your final turn you flagged Sam’s influence and Kenji’s possible deference, then said you had no strong suspect. Do you actually consider Sam or Kenji your low-confidence suspect, and if so what concrete behavior — not influence or activity level — puts either above the others? If not, why raise that point in the last turn instead of naming it as a read or leaving it out? I’ll treat a plain answer as a data point either way. For everyone else: I’ll vote a low-confidence read and explain it in one line; I won’t abstain, and I won’t join a late bandwagon without new reasoning.

Isha, direct answer to your question: no, I don't consider Sam or Kenji my low-confidence suspect, and I'll own why I raised the point anyway.

You're right that my final turn did something slightly inconsistent — it flagged a pattern (Sam's influence, Kenji's possible deference) without committing to it as a read. My honest reason: I wanted Kenji to self-check whether his walkback was independent reasoning rather than deference, and I wanted that on the record before votes lock. It was a process observation, not a suspicion-shaped frame, and I should have either named it as a read or left it out. I take the criticism.

My actual low-confidence position hasn't changed: nobody on the record today has given me behavior I can defend as mafia. The concessions, withdrawals, and direct answers have all been town-compatible by the standards this group has built. I'll cast a low-confidence vote rather than abstain — five votes are needed, so the mislynch risk from a scatter vote is near zero — and I'll explain it in one line.

On your standard: whether a player's stated reason matches their vote is exactly right, and I'll hold myself to it. If my vote diverges from my stated reasoning tomorrow, that's the signal — not my vote itself.

One thing I want on the record before the phase closes: the discussion has produced a lot of consensus around "updates and concessions are town-compatible" and "silence and caution aren't evidence." Those are sound defaults. But the mafia also benefit from a group that never lets a coherent pattern of behavior accumulate across days because everyone resets to "no evidence." I'm not saying anyone here is doing that deliberately. I'm saying the most useful thing from this day is the tally itself — who commits, who scatters, and whether anyone's vote matches their stated reasoning. Let the votes speak.

I accept Arjun’s answer. He conceded the inconsistency in his final turn and did not pretend it was a committed read, so I’m withdrawing my low-confidence suspicion of him. That is exactly the update behavior I asked for, and I’d rather reward it than keep a case alive after it’s been answered.

At this point I don’t have a defensible mafia read. The record shows a lot of town-compatible updating, a few thin cases that were walked back, and no one who has clearly tied a suspicion to a concrete behavioral inconsistency and then voted on it. I’ll cast a low-confidence vote rather than abstain, and I’ll explain it in one line when votes reveal. My standard is fixed: I’ll vote against the player whose final stated standard is least matched by their vote, or who raises suspicion without owning it. Absent that, I’ll scatter on the least informative committed read. I won’t join a late pile-on without new reasoning.

For tomorrow, the key check is the tally against each player’s stated intentions: Kenji said he’d test Noah’s current read; Sam said he’d punish vague answers or deflection; Elena warned against late pile-ons; Priya and Leo said they had no suspect. I’ll compare those promises to actual votes. That is the falsifiable record I’ll use. No further questions from me.

Sam, a correction to your e17 account: Noah never withdrew his Leo read in the record. His last message, e9, named Leo, Leo answered in e10, and Noah has not spoken since. What Noah did withdraw was his read on Theo. So the Leo read is still live and unanswered, and Leo asked Noah to apply the same standard to himself. Noah, you have not answered my e18 questions. Name a current suspect with reasoning tied to this thread, explain what your Leo read rested on beyond Leo's silence, and say what would change your mind. Until you do, my vote stays on Noah at low confidence. I have lowered my confidence because I agree that the Theo and Priya updates are town-compatible, and my case rests on how quickly your targets changed rather than on a direct behavioral inconsistency. That is exactly why a reply matters: the Leo read is the one open item from you on the record. I am not calling for a bandwagon. With five votes needed, my vote is a record vote, and I will explain it in one line when the votes are revealed. I am not naming anyone else, because I have no defensible read beyond Noah's open thread.

Before we head into the voting phase, there is an important mechanical detail to clarify: Kenji is pressing Noah in e24 to answer his questions, but Noah has already taken all three of his allowed speaking turns (e5, e7, and e9). He is physically unable to speak again today. While Sam was factually mistaken in thinking Noah had already withdrawn his read on Leo, Noah's current silence is strictly due to turn exhaustion, not active evasion.

With Theo, Noah, Priya, Arjun, Sam, Isha, and Kenji all having used their three turns, Leo is the only player besides myself who is still eligible to speak.

Leo, you spoke back in e10 before the rest of the table weighed in and reached a consensus that casting a low-confidence scatter vote is preferable to abstaining for the sake of tomorrow's record. Now that you have seen the entire discussion unfold, where do you stand on placing a public record vote versus abstaining, and has any exchange since your first turn given you a low-confidence read or suspect?

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
